summary: This work demonstrates tunable qubit-qubit coupling in a double-resonator coupler circuit using two fixed-frequency resonators (4.47 GHz and 4.80 GHz) coupled to two tunable Xmon qubits. By tuning the qubits' frequencies with DC-bias currents, the effective coupling $g_	ext{eff}$ can be modulated from a switching-off point (near zero) to approximately 5 MHz through a frequency shift of only 50 MHz, measured via two-tone spectroscopy and vacuum Rabi oscillations.
motivation: Tunable couplers enable switchable interactions and reduced ZZ crosstalk in multi-qubit processors; the double-resonator approach offers advantages over transmon couplers including simpler fabrication, reduced flux noise, and smaller physical footprint without additional control lines.
method: Two tunable qubits coupled capacitively to two common fixed-frequency resonators allow frequency-selective interactions. The effective coupling $g_	ext{eff} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda=a,b}\left(\frac{g_{\lambda 1}g_{\lambda 2}}{\Delta_{\lambda\beta}} - \frac{g_{\lambda 1}g_{\lambda 2}}{\Sigma_{\lambda\beta}}\right) + g_{12}$ was characterized in frequency domain (two-tone spectroscopy with $g_{\lambda\beta} \approx 27$–30 MHz) and time domain (vacuum Rabi oscillations) as qubit-1 frequency was swept near qubit-2 using flux pulses.
result: Anti-crossing gaps measured in two-tone spectroscopy reduce from $\sim$10 MHz to below 2 MHz and approach zero at the switching-off point (qubit-2 at 4.37 GHz); vacuum Rabi measurements confirm coupling variation with frequency detuning, showing measurable envelope modulation despite low SNR (no Josephson parametric amplifier, 25 mK base temperature).
